What got my goat about the article was the line:

Studies have found that the insanity defense is used in less than 1 percent of felony cases nationally.

Which is really only telling part of the story. A 1995 study shows that insanity pleas, while across the board did make up around less than 1% of all pleas out of a sample rate of counties, were decidedly unmarried (~82%) male (~90%), tended toward nonwhites (53.8) in their 20s (47.8) with no high school (53.9) that had a history of prior arrest (75.1), although surprisingly the rate of violent felonies including murder using the insanity plea were about on par with nonviolent pleas -- which is where I honestly expected the difference to present itself.

So the blanket statement is true (to a point, the study had to extrapolate statewide data based on acquittals and samples of counties), although where the sentiment of the article diverges from fact is the study then found that the insanity pleas had a success rate that ranged from 13.1% (Georgia) to 87.4% (Washington).

Where this case is on the far end of statistical likelihood is the man was acquitted as part of a murder in a state that as of 1995 had one of the lowest success rates for the insanity plea; it's more common that females committing non-violent crimes are acquitted using the insanity plea.

Granted, the data itself is old enough to drink, but it was the most thorough study I could find on a cursory search.
